title: Discourse on the Logic of Language
description: A poem by M. NourbeSe Philip in She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (1989): a page-spanning collage in which a stuttering verse on English as 'my mother tongue' and 'a foreign anguish' is set beside a story of a mother licking her newborn daughter, two edicts on the treatment of slaves' languages, and textbook passages on the brain.
plot_or_argument: The central verse begins 'English / is my mother tongue', then breaks down: a mother tongue is not a foreign lan lan lang, language, l/anguish, anguish, a foreign anguish. English is her father tongue, and she has no mother tongue, only a 'dumb-tongued', 'dub-tongued' speech, and she asks what she is to do. Beside it, in capitals, a narrative tells of a mother who licks her newborn daughter clean and blows her own words, her mother's words, into the child's mouth. Two edicts in italics, in the cool voice of administration, advise slave owners to mix their slaves of different language groups so that they cannot plot rebellion, and order that any slave caught speaking his native language have his tongue removed. Passages in the style of a physiology textbook describe the brain's speech centres and nineteenth-century theories of racial difference, and the poem ends with a multiple-choice test on the tongue.
narrative_structure: Several texts on the page at once, verse in the centre, the mother's story in a margin, edicts and textbook passages elsewhere, so that the page must be read in more than one direction.
literary_form: Poem (multi-voiced text of verse, prose and edicts)
meter_and_prosody: Stammering repetition and wordplay (language, languish, anguish), capitals, italics and documentary registers set against each other; collage and fragmentation.
historical_context: She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks won the Casa de las Américas Prize in manuscript and was published in 1989; it belongs to the Caribbean debates on nation language and to the feminist writing of black women in Canada.
literary_significance: Philip's most anthologised poem and a central text of Caribbean and Canadian experimental writing on language, much taught and studied.
bibliographical_notes: Published in She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (Charlottetown: Ragweed Press, 1989). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 743.
thematic_analysis: The violence of colonial and slave history embodied in language: English as the imposed father tongue and the mother tongue that survives in secret transmission between women. The poem exposes the apparent objectivity of the coloniser's discourses, legal and scientific, and makes the reader's difficulty part of its meaning.
summary: The speaker's verse on English as mother tongue and father tongue; a narrative of a mother blowing words into her child's mouth; Edicts I and II on separating slaves by language and cutting out the tongue of any slave who speaks it; scientific accounts of the speech centres of the brain; a multiple-choice question.
critical_context: Critics read it through Brathwaite's nation language, Bhabha's in-betweenness and theories of the violence of language, as deconstructing the apparent objectivity and logic of English; reviewers of the book quoted its 'foreign anguish' as its key pun.
research_notes: The publisher is general knowledge. Wikipedia also lists Discourse on the Logic of Language (1989) as a separate item, presumably a separate printing, which was not checked. Details of the edicts and textbook passages are stated from general knowledge of the text and corroborated by student and review extracts that were not cited.

title: The Prophet's Hair
description: A short story by Salman Rushdie, first published in the London Review of Books on 16 April 1981 and collected, revised, in East, West (1994). In Srinagar, a secular moneylender who comes upon the stolen relic of the Prophet Muhammad's hair becomes a tyrannical zealot, with disastrous results for his family.
plot_or_argument: In a fierce winter in Srinagar, the moneylender's son Atta goes into the city's most dangerous quarter to hire a thief and is beaten nearly to death. The story then explains. Hashim, a rich moneylender who prides himself on his rational, honourable life, found floating in the lake a silver phial holding the famous hair of the Prophet, stolen the previous morning from the shrine at Hazratbal. A collector, he decided to keep it. At once he changed: he ordered his family to read the holy book for hours each day, forbade the cinema, told terrible truths about his marriage and his mistress, insulted his son and accused his daughter Huma of lewdness, and beat her. When Atta tried to return the relic it seemed to come back to the house by itself. Huma hires the thief Sheikh Sin to steal it; but on the night, Hashim, waking, grabs a sword, rushes out, and in the darkness kills his daughter, and then himself; the injured Atta dies, and Hashim's wife goes mad. The relic is restored to the shrine, and the thief's crippled sons, miraculously cured, lose their living as beggars.
narrative_structure: A short story opening in medias res and moving back through flashback to the climactic night and an ironic coda.
meter_and_prosody: Long, rolling sentences full of clauses, wit and Kashmiri detail; magical realism handled with comic deadpan.
historical_context: The story draws on the theft of the relic from the Hazratbal shrine in December 1963 and its recovery about two weeks later; Rushdie wrote it for the London Review of Books in the year of Midnight's Children. After the Satanic Verses affair its subject gained new resonance.
literary_significance: One of Rushdie's most anthologised stories, read as a parable of religious zeal and a forecast of the themes of his later work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the London Review of Books, vol. 3, no. 7 (16 April 1981); collected in a revised version in East, West (London: Jonathan Cape, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1064.
thematic_analysis: Religious fanaticism as a possession that destroys the possessor; the clash of secular rationalism and faith; greed and the urge to collect; the comic and terrible ironies of miracles.
summary: Hashim the moneylender keeps the relic stolen from the Hazratbal shrine; its effect on him and his household; his children's plan to have it stolen back by the master thief Sheikh Sin; the night on which everything goes wrong.
research_notes: The LRB page (seen as a search extract) confirms the date and parts of the plot; the rest of the plot is stated from general knowledge of the text and agrees with study summaries that were not cited. The Hazratbal theft of 1963, the revision for East, West and its publisher are general knowledge.

title: Imaginary Homelands
description: Salman Rushdie's Imaginary Homelands: Essays and Criticism 1981-1991 (London: Granta, in association with Penguin, 1991), a collection of essays and reviews whose title essay calls the migrant the central or defining figure of the twentieth century. Norton prints two bracketed excerpts from it.
plot_or_argument: The title essay, first printed in the London Review of Books on 7 October 1982, begins from Rushdie's attempt to recover the Bombay of his childhood in Midnight's Children and argues that exiles and migrants, looking back, create not actual cities or villages but imaginary homelands, fragmentary and partial, whose broken mirror is a truth of its own. Comparing his novel with other literature of diaspora, he claims that the migrant, whether from one country, language or culture to another or from a traditional village to a modern city, is perhaps the central or defining figure of the twentieth century, and that writers of the Indian diaspora in Britain may claim English and the English tradition as their own. Other essays dispute the category of 'Commonwealth literature', review contemporary novelists, attack the politics of Thatcher's Britain and its racism, and, in the later pieces, respond to the attacks on The Satanic Verses.
narrative_structure: Essays, lectures and reviews of 1981-1991, grouped in sections by subject, with the title essay first.
meter_and_prosody: Witty, combative, conversational prose, mixing memoir, polemic and close reading.
historical_context: Published two years into the fatwa, the book gathered a decade of Rushdie's journalism, lectures and criticism, from the years of Midnight's Children to the Satanic Verses affair.
literary_significance: A key statement of migrant and postcolonial writing in Britain; its title has become a common term for the imagined homelands of diaspora.
bibliographical_notes: Imaginary Homelands: Essays and Criticism 1981-1991 (London: Granta Books, in association with Penguin, 1991). Norton's two excerpts, '[The British Indian Writer and a Dream-England]' and '[English Is an Indian Literary Language]', are selections of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on pages 747 and 750.
thematic_analysis: Migration and memory, the right of the migrant writer to English and to many traditions, the politics of Britain, India and Pakistan, and the freedom of literature.
summary: Essays on India, Pakistan and Britain, on politics (the assassination of Indira Gandhi, the 1983 general election, censorship, the Labour Party, Palestinian identity), on the Satanic Verses affair, and on writers including Naipaul, Greene, Barnes and Ishiguro, with the title essay on memory, migration and Midnight's Children.
research_notes: The essays from which Norton's two excerpts come were not identified; the second is commonly taken from "'Commonwealth Literature' Does Not Exist" (1983), which is general knowledge, not checked. The summary of the title essay beyond Wikipedia's account (the broken mirror, the claim to English), the grouping of the essays and the essays beyond those Wikipedia names are general knowledge.

title: Epilogue
description: The four-line lyric that closes Grace Nichols's first collection, I is a Long-Memoried Woman (1983): the poet has crossed an ocean and lost her tongue, but from the root of the old one a new one has sprung.
plot_or_argument: 'I have crossed an ocean / I have lost my tongue / from the root of the old one / a new one has sprung.' The poem names the crossing and the loss in its first two lines and answers them in the second two: the lost tongue is not recovered but replaced, and the replacement grows from the root of what was lost. The speaker does not say which language the new tongue is; the poem's English, plain and uncreolised, is itself part of the answer, and the title's 'Epilogue' places the four lines after the long historical sequence of the collection, as its conclusion rather than its preface.
narrative_structure: Two unrhymed couplets, the first stating the loss ('crossed', 'lost') and the second the recovery ('sprung'), so that the poem turns at its midpoint; the last line is also the last line of the collection, which gives it the force of a conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, declarative monosyllables and a nursery-rhyme simplicity; the metaphor of the tongue as a plant is carried by 'root' and 'sprung' without being explained; the poem is written in standard English, unlike the Creole poems that precede it in the collection.
historical_context: Nichols moved from Guyana to Britain in 1977, and I is a Long-Memoried Woman (1983) was published by Karnak House, the London black publisher, with a sequence spoken by an enslaved woman; the collection won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize and was dramatised for radio and film.
literary_significance: The most anthologised short poem of Nichols's first collection and a compact statement of the central preoccupation of Black British and Caribbean writing, the relation of the new English to the languages it displaced; it is one of the three poems by Nichols in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published at the end of I is a Long-Memoried Woman (London: Karnak House, 1983). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 752.
thematic_analysis: Language as the inheritance of slavery and of survival: the mother tongue is lost in the crossing, yet the new tongue grows from its root, so that loss and continuity are held together. The poem also carries the larger argument of Nichols's work, that Caribbean English is not a broken form of the coloniser's language but a new growth with its own roots.
summary: Four unrhymed lines in two couplets, spoken in the first person, which compress the history of the Middle Passage and of Caribbean English into a single image of language as a transplanted root.
research_notes: The text is quoted from the readingnorton.com reading of the poem, which prints all four lines; the poem is the closing piece of the collection as its title indicates. The reading beneath the paraphrase is the record's own.

title: The Fat Black Woman Goes Shopping
description: The best known of the Fat Black Woman poems of 1984: a comic, angry monologue in which the Fat Black Woman shops for winter clothes in a London that has nothing in her size and watches her every move.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the Fat Black Woman 'window shopping' in the winter sales, her body taking up more room than the shops allow: the choice is lean, and nothing much is to be had beyond size 14. The assistants are 'supercilious' and the mirrors conspire; she is watched as she walks, and the watching turns a private errand into a public offence. Against the grey cold and the narrow racks she sets the clothes she would buy if the world were made for her: soft, loose, brightly coloured things, a 'silky fresh' dress, a 'tumble of tropical laughter'. The poem ends by generalising the experience, so that the individual shopper becomes 'the fat black woman' who swears in Swahili, Yoruba and nation language, and the comedy of the fitting-room turns into a judgement on a country that cannot dress or see her.
narrative_structure: Six stanzas of irregular free verse in a speaking voice, moving from the street to the shop to the mirror to the imagined wardrobe and then out to the collective 'fat black woman'; the movement from 'I' to 'she' in the last stanza turns the anecdote into a representative case.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational free verse with Creole and Caribbean inflections ('she have to' for 'she has to'), comic hyperbole, a repeated refrain-like complaint and a sudden widening of scope in the last stanza; the diction is deliberately unliterary.
historical_context: The Fat Black Woman's Poems appeared from Virago in 1984, in the period of the Thatcher governments, when the Black British women's movement and the black arts movement were at their height; Nichols had come to Britain in 1977 and the Fat Black Woman poems were written as a deliberate counter to the passive, exoticised black woman of the British imagination.
literary_significance: The most famous poem of Nichols's Fat Black Woman sequence and one of the standard anthology pieces of Black British writing, widely taught in schools; it established the comic, bodily, first-person voice that made her work popular and it is one of the three Nichols poems in Norton.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Fat Black Woman's Poems (London: Virago, 1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 752.
thematic_analysis: The poem makes the shopping trip a measure of exclusion: the body that does not fit the clothes is a body the society has not planned for, and the scrutiny of the shop assistants repeats in a minor key the larger racial and sexual policing of black women in Britain. The fantasy clothes are not mere escapism but a claim on beauty and pleasure, and the closing list of languages makes the private grievance a collective one.
summary: The Fat Black Woman goes from shop to shop in the cold, is ignored or inspected by assistants, finds 'nothing much beyond size 14', and goes home to dream of the soft, bright, billowing clothes of her imagination; the last stanza widens the complaint to the black women of Britain, who swear in Swahili, Yoruba and nation language under their breath.
research_notes: The paraphrase follows the readingnorton.com reading, which quotes the key lines ('the choice is lean / Nothing much beyond size 14'; 'the fat woman swears in Swahili, Yoruba / and nation language under her breath'); the description of the imagined clothes is general knowledge of the poem rather than a quotation, since the full text was not consulted.

title: Wherever I Hang
description: A poem in Guyanese Creole from Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (1989) about settling in England: the speaker sends home photographs of herself among the pigeons and the snow, learns to queue and to warn people before visiting, and ends divided 'to de bone' between two homes.
plot_or_argument: The speaker sends home photographs of herself among the pigeons and the snow and wards off the cold; little by little she changes her 'calypso ways', learning to give clear warning before visiting anybody and to wait her turn in the queue. After all this time she has grown accustomed to English life, but she still misses 'back-home side', and to tell the truth she does not know where she belongs: she is 'divided to de ocean / divided to de bone'. The poem's last line drops the elegiac tone for a joke: 'Wherever I hang me knickers - that's my home.' The joke does the argument's work, since it makes home a matter of daily habit and the body rather than of nation or blood, and refuses the pathos the poem has just earned.
narrative_structure: Five stanzas of loose Creole verse, of unequal length; the first three accumulate the details of adaptation, the fourth turns to the speaker's uncertainty and the last delivers the joke that also concludes the argument. Each stanza begins with a connective ('And is so', 'Now', 'But') that gives the poem the air of talk.
meter_and_prosody: Guyanese Creole spelling and syntax ('mi', 'de', 'belaang', 'accustom'), an unhurried conversational rhythm, internal rhyme and assonance in place of regular metre, and a deliberate anticlimax in the last line; the register moves between the elegiac and the comic within a stanza.
historical_context: Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman was published by Virago in 1989, a decade after Nichols settled in London; the poem belongs to the large body of Caribbean-British writing of the 1980s about migration and belonging, and its Creole is the 'nation language' of Kamau Brathwaite and of the dub poets.
literary_significance: One of Nichols's most quoted poems on migration and one of the three of hers in the Norton Anthology; its last line has become a proverbial phrase in Caribbean-British writing, and the poem is a standard example of the use of Creole in English poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (London: Virago, 1989) and collected in I Have Crossed an Ocean: Selected Poems (Bloodaxe, 2010). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 753.
thematic_analysis: Home as practice rather than origin: the poem records the small disciplines of English life (queuing, appointments, warning before visits) as the materials out of which a new belonging is made, while keeping the loss of the old one in view. The divided self is stated in the 'divided to de ocean' image and then comically resolved, so that the poem neither sentimentalises exile nor pretends that assimilation is complete.
summary: Five stanzas of Creole verse in which the immigrant speaker describes her adaptation to English life, the habits she has taken on and the homesickness she cannot cure, and concludes that wherever she hangs her knickers is her home.
research_notes: The summary follows the text printed in full by the greatbritishwriters reading and the extracts quoted by readingnorton.com; the stanza count follows that text and was not checked against the 1989 printing.

title: Inglan Is a Bitch
description: The title poem of Linton Kwesi Johnson's third collection (Race Today, 1980), spoken in the voice of a Jamaican immigrant who has worked in Britain for decades and is made redundant at fifty-five; a dub poem built on the refrain 'Inglan is a bitch, dere's no escapin it'.
plot_or_argument: The speaker came to London and worked on the Underground, then as a dish-washer, then digging ditches, and found that hard work brought him nothing: after a while he stopped the overtime and put down his tools. The chorus returns: 'Inglan is a bitch, dere's no escapin it', and there is no running away from it. He works day shifts and night shifts, clean work and dirty work, while the society says that black men are lazy; if you saw how he works you'd say he was crazy. In a factory in Brackley they have done nothing for fifteen years but pack crockery, and after fifteen years' labour he falls out of favour. There is work in abundance, yet he is made redundant at fifty-five and sent to draw the dole. The poem ends by turning the complaint outward - 'is whey wi a goh dhu 'bout it?' - from a lament into a question about action.
narrative_structure: A single long monologue in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the refrain, which recurs with small variations ('dere's no escapin it', 'dere's no runnin' whey fram it', 'y'u bettah face up to it'); the movement is chronological, from arrival to redundancy, and the last line breaks the pattern with a question.
literary_form: Poem (dub poem, long line in Creole)
meter_and_prosody: Jamaican Creole transcribed for the page ('mi', 'w'en', 'bwoy', 'noh'), a heavy stress beat and long breath-lines shaped for performance over a reggae bass line; repetition and refrain instead of rhyme; documentary detail (Brackley, the dole, the tax racket) carried in the plainest diction.
historical_context: The poem was the title piece of Inglan Is a Bitch, published by Race Today Publications in 1980, the year of the Brixton uprising and of the Thatcher government's first budget; it was performed with Dennis Bovell's dub band and recorded on Bass Culture (1980). Its picture of black labour in Britain belongs to the Windrush generation's experience of the 1970s and 1980s.
literary_significance: The best known poem of British dub poetry and a standard anthology piece; its refrain passed into common speech and it is the work by which Johnson is most often represented, including in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Inglan Is a Bitch (London: Race Today Publications, 1980); recorded on the album Bass Culture (Island, 1980). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 755.
thematic_analysis: The poem is an anatomy of the exploitation of black immigrant labour: the hardest work for the least pay, the taxes that claw back the wage packet, the accusation of laziness levelled at the worker who works two shifts, and the redundancy that ends a working life. Its refrain refuses consolation: England cannot be escaped, only faced, and the final question moves from endurance to politics. The comic, proverbial force of 'bitch' carries the anger without softening it.
summary: A monologue in Jamaican Creole recounting a working life in London, from the underground and the dish-washing to a factory in Brackley and the dole, punctuated by the refrain that England is a bitch from which there is no running away.
research_notes: The paraphrase follows the text printed with the Bass Culture recording and quoted at length in the OpenEdition study; the printed collection's text was not collated against it, and the stanza division given here follows the recording's refrain pattern rather than the 1980 page setting.

title: To Room Nineteen
description: Doris Lessing's story of 1963, collected in A Man and Two Women, about Susan Rawlings, a clever, happily married mother of four who finds that her sensible life has no room for her and takes a hotel room in which to be alone, until the room too is taken from her.
plot_or_argument: The Rawlings' marriage is grounded in intelligence: they married late, 'amid general rejoicing', have four healthy children and a large white house with a garden, and manage their lives so well that they seem to have arranged an abstinence from pain. Matthew is briefly unfaithful, and the affair is absorbed as an eminently sensible arrangement; but something has been let in. When the youngest children go to school, Susan finds the house empty and herself without occupation, and a 'demon' begins to wait for her in the garden. She tries the remedies the story offers her: she takes a job, gives it up; she arranges an au pair and a cleaner; she takes a room in a hotel in Bloomsbury, room nineteen, where she sits for hours doing nothing, and comes home refreshed and able to be a wife and mother again. Matthew, unable to accept that she wants nothing but solitude, presses her for an explanation, and she invents a lover because a lover is a reason he can understand. The deception grows; he hires a private detective and believes himself betrayed. With the last place of her own discovered, Susan goes back to room nineteen, stops up the cracks of the gas fire and kills herself. The story's final paragraphs present her death not as breakdown but as a release into a 'fructifying' dark, and the narrator's judgement falls on the intelligence that could explain everything and understand nothing.
narrative_structure: A framed third-person narrative in numbered sections, beginning with a narrator's essay-like statement and ending with a lyrical account of the suicide; the narration moves between free indirect discourse inside Susan's mind and a cold, analytic view of the marriage, and the temporal frame runs from courtship to death with the detective's report as its turning point.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, exact, deliberately unadorned prose that reports feeling with clinical detachment; the key word 'sensible' recurs as a refrain; the narrator interrupts the fiction with general statements, in the manner of the eighteenth-century essay-novel; the imagery of water and of the dark river gathers towards the end.
historical_context: Written in London and published in the collection A Man and Two Women (1963), the story belongs to the moment in which the dissatisfaction of educated housewives became a public subject, four years before The Feminine Mystique. Lessing had come to England from Southern Rhodesia in 1949 and had been a member of the Communist Party until 1956; the story's analysis of marriage is continuous with the 'free women' of The Golden Notebook, which was published the year before.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised English short stories of the postwar period and a central text in the literary history of second-wave feminism; it is the Lessing story in the Norton Anthology and the one on which her account of female breakdown is most often based.
bibliographical_notes: Published in A Man and Two Women (London: MacGibbon and Kee, 1963) and collected in To Room Nineteen: Collected Stories Volume One (1978). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 764.
thematic_analysis: The story examines what a rationally arranged life leaves out: the Rawlings' intelligence is a machine for avoiding pain, and it produces a woman with no reason to live. Lessing keeps three explanations in play - the class-bound boredom of the middle-class housewife, the gender order that makes the wife's identity a function of her family, and a more general account of the sensitive soul in a sensible world - and refuses to settle the case. The invented lover is the story's sharpest stroke: a wife's need for solitude cannot be heard, so it must be translated into the language of sex that the husband and the society can understand. Room nineteen itself is the ambiguous symbol of the whole: a place of nothing, which is also the only place where Susan is herself.
summary: A third-person narrative, framed by an intrusive narrator's opening remark that this is a story about 'a failure in intelligence', which follows Susan Rawlings from her marriage and the birth of four children through her growing sense of vacancy to the rented room nineteen and her suicide.
critical_context: The story is a standing point of reference in feminist criticism of the postwar short story, read by Lessing's commentators as a case study in the 'problem that has no name' and, more recently, as a subtler text than that reading allows: critics of the 1980s and 1990s emphasised the story's refusal to choose between social, psychological and metaphysical explanations, and its careful management of a narrator who judges as well as reports. It belongs with the stories of A Man and Two Women and of To Room Nineteen, where Lessing worked out the themes that The Golden Notebook would take up on a larger scale, and it is the Lessing text most often set in courses on the modern short story.
research_notes: The plot account is drawn from the story as summarised and quoted in the Encyclopedia of the Short Story entry (encyclopedia.com) and from general knowledge of the text; quotations were checked against that entry. The interpretation of the ending is the record's own and does not follow any single critic.

title: Self-Portrait
description: A short poem from A. K. Ramanujan's first collection, The Striders (1966), in which the speaker sees, in shop windows and against the laws of optics, the portrait of a stranger who resembles everyone but himself.
plot_or_argument: 'I resemble everyone / but myself.' The speaker sometimes sees, in shop windows and despite the well-known laws of optics, the portrait of a stranger, date unknown, often signed in a corner by his father. The poem's joke is a serious one: the mirror of the shop window gives back not the self but the family, so that identity is inheritance before it is anything else. The missing date and the father's signature make the portrait an old-master likeness in a family album, and they leave the speaker unable to say when or whether he began. In fourteen lines the poem states the theme that runs through all of Ramanujan's poetry, the self as a copy of others, and it does so in an idiom so plain that the metaphysical pun on resemblance is easy to miss.
narrative_structure: A single sentence in fourteen short lines, without stanza breaks and with almost no punctuation in the middle; the syntax enacts a process of looking that never arrives at the self, and the last line's revelation ('signed in a corner / by my father') reverses the poem's direction.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, clipped free verse of two- and three-word lines; the diction is abstract and legalistic ('the well-known laws / of optics', 'date unknown'), and the flatness of the statement is what makes the last line's turn effective.
historical_context: The Striders was published by Oxford University Press in London in 1966, while Ramanujan was teaching at Chicago; the poem belongs to the first generation of Indian English poetry written by professional linguists, and its theme of family resemblance is a recurring one in his work.
literary_significance: One of the most often quoted of Ramanujan's early poems and the standard short introduction to his theme of inherited identity; it is the first of his two selections in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Striders (London: Oxford University Press, 1966) and collected in Selected Poems (1976) and The Collected Poems (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 797.
thematic_analysis: Resemblance as the ground of identity and the obstacle to it: to resemble everyone is to have no portrait of one's own, and the father's signature on the stranger's face makes inheritance both the source of the self and the reason it cannot be seen. The poem is also about the migrant's double sight, the Indian in America who finds his family in every face.
summary: A single sentence of fourteen short lines: the speaker resembles everyone but himself, sees a stranger's portrait in shop windows, dated unknown but often signed in a corner by his father.
research_notes: The text is quoted from the Selected Poetry PDF and from the University of Hyderabad introduction to Ramanujan, which print the poem complete and agree; the reading is the record's own.

title: Elements of Composition
description: The opening poem of Ramanujan's third collection, Second Sight (1986), which composes the self out of the chemical elements and then, in the second half, sets the constant elements against the moving eyes that can see only by moving.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins 'Composed as I am, like others, / of elements on certain well-known lists', and names the ingredients: the father's seed and the mother's egg gathering earth, air, fire and mostly water into a 'mulberry mass', moulding calcium, carbon, 'even gold, magnesium and such' into a chattering self tangled in love and work and scary dreams. The second half turns to what such a self can see: the eyes can see the constancy of things only by moving constantly. The poem ends with a sequence of images of constancy - a child's face, a remembered street, a woman's hand - that the moving eye catches only as it passes, so that knowledge is a matter of motion and the self a compound that knows itself only in passing. The title is a pun on two senses of 'composition': the chemical constitution of a body and the writing of a poem.
narrative_structure: A single poem in two unequal movements, the first a catalogue in short lines that accumulates the elements, the second a meditation turning on 'only by moving constantly'; the caesural line-breaks and the switch from list to argument give it the shape of a thesis and its qualification.
meter_and_prosody: Short free-verse lines, abrupt enjambments and a colloquial, apparently casual syntax ('and such', 'scary dreams') set against technical and archaic diction ('mulberry mass', 'constancy'); the list form is carried by parallelism and the poem's argument by a single turn.
historical_context: Second Sight was published in Delhi and New York by Oxford University Press in 1986, after Ramanujan's return from a stay in Sri Lanka in 1983 and his renewed reading of the Upanishads and Buddhist philosophy; the poem opens the volume and announces its changed vision.
literary_significance: The proem of Second Sight and the clearest statement of Ramanujan's late poetics of particulars and motion; with 'Self-Portrait' it is one of his two selections in the Norton Anthology and the one by which his philosophical ambition is usually introduced.
bibliographical_notes: Published as the opening poem of Second Sight (Delhi and New York: Oxford University Press, 1986) and collected in The Collected Poems (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 797.
thematic_analysis: The poem sets the fixity of the elements against the mobility of the consciousness they make, and asks what kind of knowledge a moving observer can have of a stable world. The 'well-known lists' invoke both the periodic table and the classical elements, so that the modern chemistry and the ancient cosmology compose the same body; the 'mulberry mass' and the 'chattering self' keep the tone comic and bodily. As a proem it sets out the programme of Second Sight: a poetry of particulars that knows that truth is only grasped in passing.
summary: Two movements: a list of the elements that make up the body, from the father's seed and the mother's egg through earth, air, fire and water to calcium, carbon, gold and magnesium, and then a meditation on the self so composed, 'a chattering self tangled in love and work', capable of seeing the constancy of things only by moving constantly.
research_notes: The text and the sequence of images in the second half were read in the Selected Poetry PDF, which prints the poem complete; the poem's page number in the Norton volume follows the list (797) and the second poem's exact placing was not checked.

title: Black Jackets
description: A poem from Thom Gunn's My Sad Captains (1961) about a group of young bikers in leather jackets who stand in a café and, for the length of a record, embody a style of rebellion the poet watches from outside.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins in the silence after a record ends: the red-haired boy who drove a van in weekday overalls, but like his friends, has put on his black jacket, and the group of them stand at the café counter in a dress that is a uniform and a statement. Gunn describes the jackets, the hair, the boots and the poses with the exactness of a fashion plate, and notes the self-containment of the group, its indifference to the watcher and its own internal codes. The speaker is outside this world and knows it: he records rather than joins, and the poem's sympathy is with the completeness of the style rather than with any politics it might carry. The last stanzas turn the observation into a judgement on the price of belonging to such a group, and on the outsider's freedom to leave.
narrative_structure: Eight-line stanzas in a loose iambic line, moving from the record's silence to a general reflection; the descriptive stanzas give way to a concluding meditation, and the whole is held together by the repeated image of the jackets.
meter_and_prosody: Exact, unsentimental description in plain diction; enjambment used to keep the stanza moving; a conversational, slightly clipped syntax; the rhythm of ordinary speech held in a firm stanzaic frame, characteristic of the Movement manner.
historical_context: My Sad Captains was published by Faber in 1961, when Gunn had been in California for seven years; the poem belongs to the British 'Movement' moment but its subject, the style-culture of young working-class men, already points to the American poems that follow.
literary_significance: One of the poems by which Gunn's early 'Movement' manner is represented in the Norton Anthology, and a frequently anthologised study of postwar youth style; with 'My Sad Captains' it stands for the 1961 collection.
bibliographical_notes: Published in My Sad Captains and Other Poems (London: Faber and Faber, 1961), collected in Collected Poems (1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 800.
thematic_analysis: The poem is an early study of the postwar youth style that would become the emblem of the 1960s: leather, motorcycles, a music-driven solidarity, the body turned into a sign. Gunn's interest is aesthetic and sociological at once, in how a group makes a complete world out of dress and gesture, and in what that world costs. Class is present throughout in the weekday overalls under the jackets, and the poem's calm, unpatronising tone is part of its achievement.
summary: The speaker describes the red-haired boy who drove a van and his friends in their black leather jackets, their studied poses and their music, and reflects on the self-sufficiency of their world and his own distance from it.
research_notes: The summary was written from the opening lines quoted in the poemhunter selection and from general knowledge of the poem, not from a complete text; the description of the closing stanzas is therefore general and the paraphrase claims no quotation beyond the quoted first stanza.

title: My Sad Captains
description: The title poem of Thom Gunn's 1961 collection: a night meditation in which friends, some of them with 'historical names', appear one by one in the darkness like stars, and the poet takes his leave of them.
plot_or_argument: 'One by one they appear in the darkness: a few friends, and a few with historical names.' The figures come out like stars, and the speaker notes how late they start to shine, how their light is steady and how they move apart from one another. The poem holds them in view as a constellation, a company that is also a pattern, and then acknowledges that he cannot keep them: the last lines turn from the observed group to the observer's own position, alone in the dark and free. The title's 'sad captains' derives from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, where Antony's captains desert him, and the poem quietly reverses the allusion: these captains do not desert the speaker, he leaves them, and the sadness is his own.
narrative_structure: Short quatrains, with a single sentence running through most of the poem and a turn in the last stanza from description to address; the poem's movement is from the many to the one, from the constellation to the solitary watcher.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines of three or four stresses; a lucid, almost epigrammatic syntax; the images are astronomical and maritime at once ('captains'), and the diction is deliberately plain, with the Shakespearean allusion left unglossed.
historical_context: The title poem of My Sad Captains (Faber, 1961), the collection that marked the end of Gunn's strict Movement phase and the beginning of the free-verse poems of Touch (1967); he had been in California since 1954 and the poem's solitary watcher belongs to that distance.
literary_significance: The title poem of Gunn's central early collection and a standard anthology piece; with 'Black Jackets' it represents the 1961 volume in the Norton Anthology, and its Shakespearean echo is one of the most discussed moments in his early work.
bibliographical_notes: Published as the title poem of My Sad Captains and Other Poems (London: Faber and Faber, 1961), collected in Collected Poems (1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 801.
thematic_analysis: Friendship, loss and the poet's relation to a company he cannot join: the poem is about the cost of the observer's freedom, and it reads as a farewell to the Movement's collective, the group of poets with whom Gunn had been identified. The starlight metaphor gives the friends a permanence in the poem that they do not have in life, and the act of naming them is the elegy.
summary: The speaker watches a group of friends appear in the dark, one by one, some with historical names; he notes how late they start to shine, how they drift, and how he must part from them, and the poem ends with his acceptance of the separation.
research_notes: The opening is quoted from the poemhunter text; the account of the closing lines is based on general knowledge and on the poem's reported argument, and the Antony and Cleopatra allusion is a standard observation rather than a quotation from a critic.

title: From the Wave
description: A poem from Thom Gunn's Moly (1971) describing surfers riding a wave off the California coast, in which the balance of the riders becomes an image of the discipline and surrender of the poetic art.
plot_or_argument: The wave mounts at sea like a concave wall and pushes forward; from hiding the black shapes of the surfers rise into sight on their boards. Their pale feet poise with a learned skill, and it is the wave they imitate that keeps them so still: for seconds the marbling bodies are half wave, half men. They wait as late as they can and then slice the face of the water in timed procession, for 'balance is triumph in this place, / triumph possession'. The mindless heave they rode breaks as they leave it and loses itself; their bodies loosen, and the bare foot feels the suck of shingle. They paddle in the shallows, splash each other, and swim out to wait for the right waves to gather. The poem's grammar keeps the wave as the subject even while the men act, so that the surfers are a function of the sea rather than its masters, and their skill is described as an imitation of what they ride.
narrative_structure: Six eight-line stanzas rhyming ababcdcd, moving through the wave's cycle from its mounting to its breaking and the swimmers' return; the regular stanza is itself an image of the balance the poem describes.
meter_and_prosody: Firmly metred eight-line stanzas with a buoyant rhythm; liquid consonant clusters and long vowels ('mottles', 'shingle', 'suck') imitate the water; the diction is physical and exact, with almost no abstraction; the tone is absorbed and unironic.
historical_context: Moly (1971) was written in California, in the period of Gunn's looser free-verse experiments, but 'From the Wave' keeps a strict stanza; its subject, the surfing culture of the Pacific coast, is one of the poems by which Gunn's American life entered his English work.
literary_significance: One of Gunn's most admired descriptions and a standard anthology piece from Moly; it is in the Norton Anthology as the representative poem of his American middle period.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Moly (London: Faber and Faber, 1971), collected in Collected Poems (1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 801.
thematic_analysis: Surfing is an image of the artist's relation to a power he does not own: the riders imitate the wave, hold to its form, and are released when it breaks. 'Balance is triumph ... triumph possession' states the poem's ethic, that mastery consists in a momentary agreement with a force larger than the self. The writing also carries Gunn's pleasure in surfaces and contact, the substance of bodies brought against the substance of water.
summary: The wave mounts and the surfers appear on their boards, holding still against its face, half wave and half men, until they slide down it and paddle out to wait for the next; the poem watches the whole cycle of the wave from its building to its breaking.
research_notes: The text was read complete in the poemhunter printing, and the stanzaic description follows it; the reading of the poem's argument is the record's own.

title: Still Life
description: An elegy from The Man with Night Sweats (1992) for a friend dying of AIDS: the poet sits at the hospital bed of a man whose body has become a still life, and watches for the breath he cannot give up.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins 'I shall not soon forget', and gives the details: the angle of the friend's head, wrenched sideways as he lay and stared unseeing at the wall; the greyish-yellow skin; the mouth held open by the tube 'in an astonished O'. The title's pun runs through the poem: the friend is a still life in the painter's sense, an arrangement of objects, and he is still alive, still breathing, 'a life-long breather' as the poem says with bitter irony. The watcher cannot help him and cannot leave, and the poem ends on the image of the tube and the astonished mouth, which is both a clinical detail and an accusation. Gunn's elegy refuses consolation and refuses horror: it holds the dying body in view with the same exactness he gave to the surfers of 'From the Wave'.
narrative_structure: Short four-line stanzas, loosely rhymed, in which each stanza gives one detail of the bedside scene; the poem's progress is not narrative but a sequence of perceptions held under the pressure of memory, and the closing image returns to the mouth.
meter_and_prosody: Spare, exact, unornamented language with a strong iambic base; the rhyme is irregular and often off-rhyme; the syntax is clipped and the tone level, so that the horror is carried by the precision rather than by exclamation.
historical_context: The Man with Night Sweats (Faber, 1992) was written as Gunn's friends in San Francisco died of AIDS; the collection won the Lenore Marshall Poetry Prize and is the central book of AIDS elegies in English. 'Still Life' is a memorial for Larry Hoyt, as Neil Powell's obituary of Gunn states.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised poems of The Man with Night Sweats and, with 'The Missing', the representative of Gunn's AIDS elegies in the Norton Anthology; the collection is credited with restoring poetry to a public role in the crisis.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Man with Night Sweats (London: Faber and Faber, 1992), collected in Collected Poems (1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 802.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the body of a friend transformed by illness into something the watcher can only describe; the pun on 'still life' insists on the continuity between the dying man and the objects of a painting, and the poem's tenderness lies in the precision of its looking. It is also a poem about helplessness, the watcher's position at the bedside, and about the AIDS epidemic as a daily experience of hospitals and tubes rather than of public rhetoric.
summary: A bedside poem in short rhyming stanzas: the dying friend's greyish-yellow skin, the angle of his head wrenched sideways, the tube in his mouth, and the poet's inability to look away or to forget.
research_notes: The phrases quoted ('I shall not soon forget', 'greyish-yellow skin', the tube 'in an astonished O') are taken from the text as printed in Neil Powell's Guardian obituary and in the New York Times review; the dedication to Larry Hoyt is stated by Powell.

title: The Missing
description: The central elegy of The Man with Night Sweats: watching his friends die of AIDS, the poet sees himself as a half-finished statue, outside the warm network of friendships that is disappearing around him.
plot_or_argument: 'Now as I watch the progress of the plague, / The friends surrounding me fall sick, grow thin, / And drop away.' The speaker asks whether his own shape is less vague now, bared and sharply exposed, and answers that he does not like the statue's chill contour, not nowadays: the warmth that used to invest him went outward through mind and limb and feeling in an 'involved increasing family'. Contact of friend led to another friend, a 'supple entwinement through the living mass' which might have had no end and was an image of an unlimited embrace. Now the entwinement is broken and the speaker is left as the statue, defined by the loss of those who made him. The poem's title carries both senses: the friends are missing, and the speaker is one of the missing, a survivor who has been left outside the company that gave him his shape.
narrative_structure: Three twelve-line stanzas, unrhymed but metrically regular, moving from the observation of the dying friends to the self-scrutiny of the statue and then to the remembered embrace; the poem's argument is carried by a single extended comparison rather than by narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in long stanzas, with a grave, measured movement; the diction is abstract and sculptural ('shape', 'contour', 'definition') set against bodily words ('supple', 'entwinement', 'warmth'); the tone is elegiac without being rhetorical.
historical_context: Written in San Francisco in the late 1980s and published in The Man with Night Sweats (1992); the poem's image of the statue and its 'living mass' belongs to the Gay Liberation culture of the 1970s as much as to the epidemic that followed it, and the collection is a document of the AIDS years.
literary_significance: One of the central poems of The Man with Night Sweats and the longest of Gunn's AIDS elegies to be anthologised; with 'Still Life' it is his representation in the Norton Anthology and the poem most often cited for the collection's vision of community.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Man with Night Sweats (London: Faber and Faber, 1992), collected in Collected Poems (1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 803.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about identity as relation: the speaker's self was made by the network of friends and lovers, and their deaths leave him not more himself but less. The statue image reverses the usual consolation of elegy, since what survives is cold and defined only by absence. The 'unlimited embrace' gives the gay community of San Francisco a value that the poem states without apology, and the plague is named as a plague, a public catastrophe experienced privately.
summary: Three stanzas of twelve lines in which the speaker watches the plague thin the circle of his friends, feels his own shape grow sharper and colder as they die, and remembers the 'supple entwinement' of the community that is being destroyed.
research_notes: The poem's first lines and the 'supple entwinement' passage are quoted from the text printed in the New York Times review and in Neil Powell's Guardian obituary; the stanza description follows those texts and was not checked against the 1992 printing.

title: A Far Cry from Africa
description: Derek Walcott's best-known early poem, collected in In a Green Night (1962): a meditation on the Mau Mau rebellion in Kenya which asks how a Caribbean poet of African and European descent can take sides in the violence of decolonisation.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens on the Mau Mau fighters, described as 'gorillas' wrestling with the British, and sets the brutality of the uprising against the rhetoric of empire; the 'white child' is speared in his bed while the Kikuyu 'dance' and the English language is spoken over the dead. Walcott refuses the division: he is 'poisoned with the blood of both', and the poem turns on the question of how to choose between an Africa that is his inheritance and the English tongue that is his instrument. 'How choose / Between this Africa and the English tongue I love?' The stanzas move rapidly between scenes and registers, from the documentary violence of the rebellion to the lyric address to a 'drunken officer of the Empire', and end with the poet's confession that he will die 'in a country / Where the trees are tall and the rivers are wide', neither wholly African nor wholly English. The title's 'far cry' is both distance and protest, the cry from far away and the difference that cannot be closed.
narrative_structure: Three eight-line stanzas of loose pentameter with an irregular rhyme scheme; the poem moves by sudden transitions between the African and English scenes, and its argument is carried by rhetorical questions and apostrophes rather than by narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Rich, allusive, syntactically complex verse, with the English literary inheritance (the Bible and Shakespeare) heard in the cadence; hard consonants and violent verbs for the rebellion; the mature Walcott's habit of holding two languages and two histories in a single sentence is already present.
historical_context: Written in the 1950s and collected in In a Green Night: Poems 1948-1960 (Cape, 1962), the poem responds to the Mau Mau emergency in Kenya (1952-1960), the most violent episode of British decolonisation in Africa, and to Walcott's own mixed inheritance in Saint Lucia.
literary_significance: Walcott's most frequently anthologised early poem and the standard introduction to his theme of the divided colonial self; it is the first of his four selections in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the collection In a Green Night: Poems 1948-1960 (London: Jonathan Cape, 1962); the date of its first periodical publication was not established, so the poem is dated by its collection. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 804.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a study of the divided colonial subject: Walcott, descended from English and African Caribbean ancestors, can neither disown the English language nor accept the empire that brought it, and the Mau Mau emergency makes that division a matter of life and death. The refusal to take a side is not neutrality but a historical condition, and the poem's force lies in its refusal to resolve it into comfort. Race, violence and language are shown to be one question.
summary: Three eight-line stanzas on the Kikuyu and the British in Kenya: the 'gorillas' of the Mau Mau, the colonist with his English tongue, and the speaker's divided inheritance, which leaves him unable either to condemn the violence or to accept the empire that provoked it.
research_notes: The paraphrase follows the text as quoted in the Oxford Research Encyclopedia and the Connotations article, which print the opening and the 'How choose' question; the exact date of first publication is given as 1962 in the Norton list, and no earlier printing was found, so the record follows the collection.

title: The Schooner Flight
description: The long monologue of Shabine, a mixed-race sailor who leaves Trinidad on the schooner Flight, from The Star-Apple Kingdom (1979): Walcott's most ambitious poem before Omeros and the fullest statement of his vision of Caribbean identity, spoken in eleven sections by a man who is 'either nobody, or a nation'.
plot_or_argument: Shabine introduces himself as 'a rusty head sailor with sea-green eyes' whom they nickname Shabine, 'the patois for any red nigger', a man with Dutch, African and English blood who had a sound colonial education and is 'either nobody, or a nation'. He fights with his wife Maria Concepcion and leaves Trinidad on the schooner Flight, and the poem follows the voyage through the islands from Monos to Nassau. As he sails, Shabine remembers the history of the archipelago: the Amerindian past, the plantations, the massacres of colonial rule, the corruption of the new states, and his own love for the sea and for the ordinary people of the islands. He reflects on the poet's vocation, on language and on the colour line that cuts through his own family, and in the last sections his voice moves out of the frame of the narrative altogether: 'Shabine sang to you from the depths of the sea.' The poem's eleven sections are held together by the speaking voice rather than by a plot, and its model is the Odyssey (Shabine, like Odysseus, is 'nobody') as much as the Caribbean ballad and the calypso. Along the way the poem registers the corruption of the independent Caribbean states, the continuities of colonial power and the ordinary decency of the people Shabine sails among, and its narrator's voice is by turns boastful, tender, furious and elegiac, so that the single monologue holds the whole archipelago in view without ever settling into a single judgement of it.
narrative_structure: Eleven numbered sections in a flexible pentameter, spoken by Shabine and interrupted by quoted speech, song and invective; the narrative is recursive rather than linear, returning to the quarrel with Maria and to the history of the islands, and the last section dissolves the narrative frame into pure song.
meter_and_prosody: A flexible, muscular pentameter carrying the spoken idiom of the islands ('I had a sound colonial education') and the high rhetoric of the English literary tradition in the same breath; a rapid succession of registers, from calypso comedy to prophetic denunciation; the sea imagery gives the poem its recurring music.
historical_context: Published in The Star-Apple Kingdom (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1979; Cape, 1980), the poem belongs to Walcott's Trinidad years and to the moment of Black Power and the New Jewel Movement in the Caribbean; it is the poem in which he worked out the long narrative form that Omeros would take up in 1990.
literary_significance: Walcott's major poem of the 1970s and the work in which his Caribbean everyman, Shabine, is created; it is the poem by which his ambition to write a Caribbean epic is usually dated, and a central text of postcolonial poetry in English. Its pentameter and its speaking sailor are the direct preparation for Omeros, and its 'either nobody, or a nation' has become the most quoted line in Walcott's work.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Star-Apple Kingdom (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1979; London: Jonathan Cape, 1980), with sections collected in Selected Poems (2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 805.
thematic_analysis: Identity without a single origin: Shabine's mixed descent, which denies him a place in either the black or the white society of the islands, becomes the ground of a representative Caribbean self, 'either nobody, or a nation'. The poem sets the beauty of the sea and the islands against the violence of their history, and makes the poet's song the only form of belonging that survives. Exile is both the wound and the condition of the poetry, and the final transformation of the speaker into a voice singing from the sea turns loss into art.
summary: Eleven sections in the voice of Shabine, a sailor nicknamed for the patois for a 'red nigger', who quarrels with his wife Maria Concepcion, goes to sea on the Flight, remembers the colonial history of the islands and the massacres of the past, and ends by singing from the depths of the sea.
critical_context: Fuller and later Caribbean critics have made 'The Schooner Flight' the test case for Walcott's politics of identity, reading Shabine's mixed descent as a rejection of both Black Power's and the colonial order's claims on him; others have objected that the poem's solution, the transformation of the speaker into pure song, evades the political questions it raises. Its relation to Omeros has been central to that debate, since the later poem expands the sailor's monologue into an epic and gives his 'nobody or a nation' a whole archipelago to inhabit.
research_notes: The passages quoted ('I'm just a red nigger who love the sea', 'either I'm nobody, or I'm a nation', 'Shabine sang to you from the depths of the sea') are taken from Mary C. Fuller's Connotations article and the Oxford Research Encyclopedia; the section-by-section account is based on that article and on general knowledge, not on a complete reading of the 1979 text.

title: The Season of Phantasmal Peace
description: The short visionary poem that closes The Fortunate Traveller (1981): an imagined peace in which all the birds of the world carry the light through the dark, and the nations are, for a moment, reconciled.
plot_or_argument: The poem imagines all the birds of the world - the shearlings, the albatross, the 'dark-chanting' pigeons, the birds of every continent - gathering in one place and carrying the light between them through the night, as the nations of the world cannot. Walcott asks the season of phantasmal peace to come, and describes the procession of birds as a 'net' of wings that draws the sea and the light together. The peace is 'phantasmal' because it exists only in the vision of the poem, and the poem's beauty is inseparable from its awareness that the vision is not history. The last stanzas hold the moment of reconciliation as long as the poem can, and then release it; the birds return to their ordinary lives and the poem ends with the image of their flight, which is also the poem's own motion.
narrative_structure: Five stanzas of long unrhymed lines, moving from the gathering of the birds to the address to the season and then to the release; the poem's structure is that of a vision that is granted and then withdrawn, and the single sentence that runs through the first stanzas enacts the continuity of the flight.
meter_and_prosody: Long, incantatory free-verse lines with heavy internal assonance and a liturgical cadence; the diction oscillates between the technical names of birds and the abstract language of vision ('phantasmal', 'peace'); the syntax is elaborate and the imagery sustained, with almost no plot.
historical_context: The Fortunate Traveller (1981) was Walcott's first book of poems written with his new American academic life in view, and this poem, which closes it, is his most explicit visionary statement; the critic Mervyn Morris called it a 'vision of universal love', and other readers have seen in it the limit of the high style.
literary_significance: Walcott's most discussed short visionary poem and the last of his four selections in the Norton Anthology; it is the poem in which his late style, with its long lines and liturgical movement, is most clearly on display.
bibliographical_notes: Published as the closing poem of The Fortunate Traveller (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1981; London: Faber and Faber, 1982), collected in Selected Poems (2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 807.
thematic_analysis: A vision of peace that knows itself to be a vision: the poem sets the unity of the natural world, in which the birds of every continent share a single flight, against the divisions of the human one, and offers the poem itself as the only place where the reconciliation can be seen. The religious language ('phantasmal', the light, the net of wings) is used without orthodox belief, and the poem's sadness comes from the gap between the image and the world.
summary: A sequence of images in which the birds of many species come together, carrying a light through the darkness, and the poem addresses the 'season of phantasmal peace' that they bring, a peace that is neither of this world nor wholly beyond it.
research_notes: The account follows the Oxford Research Encyclopedia, which quotes Mervyn Morris's phrase and describes the poem as the book's closing visionary piece, and the poem's own reported imagery; the complete text was not consulted and the description of individual birds is therefore general.

title: Omeros
description: Derek Walcott's epic of Saint Lucia, published in 1990: in seven books and sixty-four chapters of terza rima, the fishermen Achille and Philoctete, the housemaid Helen and the poet's alter ego traverse the island, Africa, Europe and North America, and Homer is rewritten from the Caribbean.
plot_or_argument: Omeros opens with Philoctete's wound, a leg ulcer he attributes to the curse of the Middle Passage, and with the fishermen Achille and Hector competing for Helen, the island's Helen of Troy. Walcott's narrator, a St Lucian poet living in the United States, moves between the island and his memories of his father, his travels in Europe and America, and the history of the Caribbean; in the middle books Achille sails to Africa in a vision and encounters his enslaved ancestors, while the poet visits Dublin, Lisbon and London and meets a blind woman, Ma Kilman, whose shop and church heal Philoctete. The poem's seven books close with a sequence of farewells: Hector is killed in a bus crash, Helen and Achille are reconciled, and the poet returns to the island and to the sea, which is the poem's true subject. The Homeric frame is neither a mask nor a joke: the Odyssey supplies the pattern of voyage and return, the Iliad the quarrel over Helen, and Walcott rewrites both so that the Caribbean is the centre and Homer one of its ancestors. Walcott's seven books carry the action through a hurricane, a village festival and the death of a major character, and each of them closes in a different key, from the comedy of the market to the elegy of the final voyage home, so that the poem's epic scale is matched by a lyric attentiveness to the ordinary detail of island life. The narrative returns repeatedly to the sea, the poem's first and last subject, and to the figure of the poet himself, whose memories of his father and of his own divided education are woven into the story of the fishermen.
narrative_structure: Seven books and sixty-four chapters, mostly in terza rima, with lyric interludes and passages of prose-like narrative; the narrative is polyphonic, moving between the fishermen, Helen, the poet and historical figures, and its time is cyclical rather than linear, so that the epic voyage and the middle passage are present in the same moment.
meter_and_prosody: Terza rima in English, with a flexible pentameter and a high proportion of enjambment; a diction that mixes the fishermen's Creole with the elaborate rhetoric of the European epic; sustained metaphors of the sea, the wound and the sword; a syntax of long, suspended sentences; the poem's line is its most distinctive achievement.
historical_context: Published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux in 1990, the poem was written in St Lucia, Trinidad and Boston over the 1980s and marks Walcott's response to the quincentenary of 1492 and to the debate over the Caribbean's history; it was awarded the W. H. Smith Literary Award and is the work for which he is most often said to have deserved the Nobel Prize, which came in 1992.
literary_significance: The major long poem of the anglophone Caribbean and one of the central English poems of the late twentieth century; it reopened the epic as a form available to postcolonial writing and gave Saint Lucia its national poem. Norton prints an extract, and the record covers the whole work.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1990 by Farrar, Straus and Giroux (New York) and Faber and Faber (London); seven books, sixty-four chapters. Norton prints an extract beginning on page 808; this record covers the whole poem.
thematic_analysis: History and the uses of the past: the poem insists that the Middle Passage is not a gap in the record but the origin of the Caribbean present, and it gives the wound of Philoctete a historical as well as a mythic meaning. Race and the colonial inheritance are explored through the mixed descent of the characters and of the narrator, and exile and return through the poet's own double life in America. Language is a theme throughout: the poem asks what an epic in English can be when English is the language of the coloniser, and answers by writing the island's speech into terza rima.
summary: A long narrative poem that interweaves the lives of the St Lucian fishermen Achille and Philoctete and the beautiful Helen with the poet's own memories of his island, his travels in Europe and America, and his meditations on history, language and the sea; its characters bear Homeric names and its form is modelled on the epic.
critical_context: Omeros was received as the major long poem of the Caribbean and has generated a large criticism on its relation to Homer, to Dante's terza rima and to the epic tradition, and on its politics of history and race; admirers treat its fusion of Creole speech and classical form as the fulfilment of Walcott's lifelong project, while sceptical readers have questioned the epic's treatment of women and its elegiac relation to the colonial past. Its place beside Derek Walcott's Nobel Prize of 1992 is secure, and it is now the work by which the twentieth-century English epic is usually measured.
research_notes: The account of the seven books and of the main characters follows Wikipedia and the Oxford Research Encyclopedia and is stated at the level of the poem's overall design; no chapter-by-chapter reading was attempted, and the description of particular episodes is limited to those documented in those sources.

title: Wind
description: A poem from Ted Hughes's first collection, The Hawk in the Rain (1957): a night of wind on the moor seen from inside a house that seems to be at sea, in which the storm becomes an image of a power the human world cannot withstand.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the famous line 'This house has been far out at sea all night', and gives the wind a body: the woods crash through darkness, the hills boom, and the winds stampede the fields 'floundering black astride and blinding wet'. Day rises under an orange sky and the hills have new places; the wind wields a 'blade-light, luminous black and emerald', flexing like the lens of a mad eye. At noon the speaker scales along the house side to the coal-house door and looks up through wind 'that dented the balls of my eyes'; the tent of the hills drums and strains its guy-rope, the skyline is 'a grimace' about to bang and vanish, a magpie is flung away and a black-backed gull bends like an iron bar. The house rings 'like some fine green goblet in the note / That any second would shatter it', and the poem ends indoors: the people sit deep in chairs before the fire, gripping their hearts, unable to entertain book, thought or each other, watching the window tremble to come in and hearing the stones cry out under the horizons.
narrative_structure: Five eight-line stanzas rhyming abbaacca or with a loose variant, moving from the night through dawn and noon to evening indoors; the poem's action is a single storm watched from one house, and its repetitions (the house, the hills, the fire) give it the feel of a refrain.
meter_and_prosody: Heavy stresses and dense consonantal clusters ('booming', 'floundering', 'flung'); an imagery of ships, tents, blades and glass drawn from the moorland world; the personification of the wind as a living body; a syntax of long suspended sentences released at the stanza's end.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1950s when Hughes was living in Cambridge and then in Yorkshire, and collected in The Hawk in the Rain (Faber, 1957), the book that won the New York Poetry Center award and made him the most talked-about young poet in England; the poem's weather belongs to the Pennine landscape of his childhood.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised poems of Hughes's first book and the standard example of his early nature writing; it is the first of his six selections in the Norton Anthology and the one that establishes the elemental weather of his imagination.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Hawk in the Rain (London: Faber and Faber, 1957), collected in Selected Poems (1972) and Collected Poems (2003). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 812.
thematic_analysis: The wind is the poem's absolute: it takes the house out to sea, rewrites the landscape and reduces human company to silence in front of a fire. Hughes's interest is in the energy that the human world cannot domesticate, and the poem's images are all of containment about to fail, the goblet, the tent, the trembling window. The firelit interior at the end is not a refuge but the measure of the storm outside, and the poem's power comes from the exchange of scales by which a house becomes a ship and the hills a tent.
summary: Five eight-line stanzas describing a night and a day of gale: the house 'far out at sea all night', the woods crashing, the hills displaced under an orange sky, the poet struggling to the coal-house door, and the family sitting in front of the fire feeling the roots of the house move.
research_notes: The poem was read complete in the Wondering Minstrels printing; the paraphrase quotes its first line and the phrases 'floundering black astride and blinding wet', 'dented the balls of my eyes' and 'like some fine green goblet', which that text and the Collected Poems contents agree on.
